findings.where: explain, paragraph 3 ("Textbooks add that the same rule is often written y = ax + b")
findings.what: This sentence has no footnote and says "textbooks often" without naming one. Cite HELM Workbook 2 ("In the linear function f(x) = ax + b, a is the gradient and b is the vertical intercept") and MCA 4.9 (SECONDARY), both already in research-notes.md, and say who writes it that way instead of "often".

findings.where: step 1 text ("From there each 1 along adds 2, so the line's rule is y = 2x + 1")
findings.what: The screen skips the step that makes the rule hold at every x: x along from the crossing, the line has climbed 2 × x above 1. The explain has this clause, but the screen does not.

findings.where: step 5 (Number first), the test point P
findings.what: P has a drag ring and lights up "on the line", but no words name it or invite him to drag it. This is the lesson's only movable test point, which the brief promised, so add one clause such as "Drag P: it lights only where 3 − 2 × x gives its y."
Why 3 − 2x can be written −2x + 3 is not said. One clause would do: 3 − 2x is 3 add −2x, and the two terms can swap places.

c slides back to 1 without a readout row. For about a second the last row still says "Slide c to −3: y = 2x − 3" while the line and its c label are back on y = 2x + 1. Either add a "Back to c = 1" row or turn m from y = 2x − 3.

Every puzzle is a three-way pick. None asks him to set the c and m handles to a given rule, which is the brief's "Draw a line from its rule: start at c and step m up for each 1 along", so the handles are never used to answer anything.

The handles can be dragged and have rings, but only step 3's words say so. A short invitation on each would help, e.g. "Slide c and watch the diamond move" on step 7 and "Turn m and the gap stops being the same" on step 9.

Two promises from the brief are on no screen. One is the screen showing y = ax + b as the same rule in the MCA's letters (it is only a sentence in the explain). The other is Celsius to Fahrenheit. Carry y = ax + b into lesson 5, where the law y = ax + b is taught, or add it to step 11's note.

c is called "the intercept" and the other crossing "the x-intercept". Say once that c is also called the y-intercept or vertical intercept (HELM's word), so the two names pair clearly and match what college texts use.
The plumber's £40 and £30 are announced from step 1, before any plumber appears, and they give away the last puzzle's numbers. Label them as example values in step 13's task instead.
The caption repeats the readout note ("m is the climb for each 1 along, and c is where the line crosses the y-axis") word for word, so it appears twice on every screen.

findings.where: readout heading "y = mx + c", every step
findings.what: y and c are italic but mx is upright, because the italics pattern skips letters that sit next to another letter. The letters in the lesson's main formula are set inconsistently.
The c dot touches the "40" tick. That tick is the number he reads c from, since the c label is held back as "?". It is legible but crowded, so give it a few pixels.

The opening shows only the line, A and B, with three blank reserved rows in the readout. The c dot and step arrive by 1.5 s, but nothing on this screen can be moved, although the lead promises handles. The first handle he can drag is on step 3.
